A low-budget horror film produced by Evil Dead director Sam Raimi has topped the North American box office.
Boogeyman, which focuses on a man who returns to his childhood home to confront his traumatic past, took $19.5m (£14.9m) in three days. Last week's chart-topper, the Robert de Niro thriller Hide and Seek, fell to number four. Other new entries included The Wedding Date, a comedy starring Will and Grace's Debra Messing, at number two.

Other Oscar contenders, including The Aviator and Sideways, continued to perform strongly at the box office. The Aviator has taken $75m (£40m) so far, while Sideways has taken $46.8m (£24.8m) in a more limited release.
Boogeyman, which cost just $7m (£3.5m) to make, performed well even though it was not screened to critics before release - normally a sign that a film will get bad reviews or perform poorly at the box office. "I certainly believe it's a genre where people are going to be more moved by the marketing materials for the movie than by what the critics say," said Rory Bruer, head of distribution for Sony Pictures, which released the film in the US. Overall the weekend box office was strong despite the fact that it was American football's Super Bowl weekend - a time when cinema admissions generally fall. This year, the top 12 films grossed around $91m (£48.3m), compared to 2004's Super Bowl weekend when the total box office was $73.4m (£38.9m).

In this paper, we investigate the impact of color constancy errors on deep neural network performance and propose a novel approach to adress these errors. Color constancy is the ability of a visual system to percieve colors independently of the illumination conditions, but deep neural networks (DNNs) are not inherently equipped with this capability. As a result, DNNs can be fooled by changes in lighting conditions that alter the color appearance of objects in an image or video.

We conduct experiments using several state-of-the-art DNN architectures and demonstrate that color constancy errors can significantly degrade their performance on tasks such as object recognition and scene understanding. We then propose a simple yet effective method to adress these errors by incorporating color constancy cues into the training process. Our approach uses a physics-based color transformation model to simulate various lighting conditions, and exposes the network to multiple versions of each input image that have been transformed under different lighting conditions. This enables the network to learn color-invariant features that are less susceptible to color constancy errors.

Our results show that our proposed method improves the robustness of DNNs against color constancy errors, leading to improved performance on object recognition and scene understanding tasks. Additionally, we analyze the contribution of different components of our method and provide insights into the role of color constancy in DNN performance. Overall, our work highlights the importance of considering color constancy when designing and evaluating DNNs for visual perception tasks, and provides a practical solution for mitigating the negative effects of color constancy errors.

When you receive a new review, it’s like opening a surprise gift—you’re filled with excitement, anticipation, and maybe even a little anxiety. But here’s the thing: reviews, whether glowing or critical, are not strict rules to live by. They’re more like compass needles, pointing you toward improvement or reaffirming your strengths. So, don’t treat them as commandments carved in stone. Instead, see them as helpful little elves offering guidance. And remember, the elves are here to help, not to judge!

Positive reviews are like warm hugs on a chilly day—heartwarming and delightful. When someone praises your work, it’s easy to feel like dancing on the ceiling. But here’s the kicker: always, always say thank you. A simple “Thank you” goes a mile, but a heartfelt “Thank you so much for your kind words!” can feel like a golden crown on your head. If the reviewer dives deep into your story, take a bow! Celebrate their insights with enthusiasm. After all, they’ve taken the time to flip to the other side of the bright reviewing penny, showing you where you’ve truly shone.

Now, let’s talk about the trickier stuff—negative reviews. These can feel like a punch to the gut, but here’s the twist: they’re a treasure trove of gold. Constructive criticism is like a map to buried treasure, guiding you toward improvement. If someone points out something you intended, acknowledge it gracefully. Say, “Thank you for noticing that detail!” It’s like giving them a gold star for their eagle eyes. And if they suggest finding a beta reader, take that advice seriously. Beta readers are like literary bodyguards, protecting your story from plot holes and inconsistencies.

Speaking of beta readers, they’re a game-changer. Before you invite them into your creative world, do your homework. Check out their previous work. It’s like bringing in a contractor to renovate your house—you want to see their portfolio first! A good beta reader can turn your rough draft into a polished gem. But remember, even the best beta readers can’t turn a lead balloon into a hot air balloon. So, choose wisely and communicate clearly.

And then there are the “not-reviews.” These are the ones that feel more like a personal essay on the reviewer’s life than feedback on your story. They’re unhelpful, bias-laden, and often frustrating. When you encounter one, resist the urge to write a novel in response. Instead, flip to the other side of the bright reviewing penny and laugh. Send a polite “Thank you for your time,” and move on. After all, you can’t make a silk purse out of a sow’s ear, so why bother? Keep your sense of humor and carry on.

In the end, responding to reviews is like juggling fire. It’s exhilarating, a bit risky, and requires constant balance. But with gratitude, grace, and a touch of humor, you’ll navigate the reviews like a pro. Remember, every review, good or bad, is a gift. So, say thank you, learn, grow, and keep writing until the ink runs out!

In the 19th century, the Afro-Portuguese exerted significant influence in central Angola, dominating semi-autonomous kingdoms that bordered coastal ports. These mestiço communities, though technically under Portuguese sovereignty, operated with a degree of local autonomy governed by prominent mestiço families. Despite their mixed European and African heritage, the Afro-Portuguese consciously distanced themselves from indigenous African populations, viewing themselves as a distinct entity due to their unique socio-cultural and economic status.

As the 19th century progressed into the early 20th, a socio-cultural transformation unfolded, as Afro-Portuguese families integrated with Kimbundu-speaking groups, leading to the formation of the modern Mbundu ethnic identity. This transition was marked by intermarriage and cultural assimilation, reshaping the sociopolitical landscape of the region. The historical dominance of the Afro-Portuguese, however, had sown the seeds of division between the coastal inhabitants and the inland communities, contributing to the complex social fabric that would later influence post-colonial conflicts.

The late 1800s saw increased external pressure from British and German colonial ambitions, which compelled the Portuguese to reassess their colonial strategies. In response to these pressures, direct Portuguese control became the norm, supplanting the previous system of indirect rule. This shift significantly affected the economic prowess of the Afro-Portuguese, particularly those engaged in the lucrative caravan trade across the interior. The advent of modern transportation technology further eroded their economic influence, altering the dynamics of commerce and power within the region.

Simultaneously, the Portuguese implemented a colonial assimilation policy to delineate social hierarchy, distinguishing between indígena and assimilado populations. Assimilados, which comprised established Afro-Portuguese families and Africans educated by missionaries, were granted certain political rights and citizenship. This categorization was contingent upon meeting specific cultural and educational criteria, reflecting the colonial state's attempt to create a stratified society. The assimilation policy, while ostensibly promoting integration, ultimately reinforced divisions and highlighted the enduring legacy of the Afro-Portuguese era on the evolving political and cultural identity of Angola.

The delay in Rittenhouse's trial comes as the United States continues to grapple with the broader implications of the Black Lives Matter movement and incidents involving police violence. The legal proceedings against Rittenhouse have become a microcosm of the national debate on race, justice, and the role of firearms in public discourse.

Judge Schroeder acknowledged the significance of the case, stating, "This is not a run-of-the-mill case. It has attracted a lot of attention, and we want to make sure everything is done correctly." The November 1 trial date sets the stage for a renewed examination of the events that transpired in Kenosha last year. Madhava of Sangamagrama was an Indian mathematician-astronomer who lived in the 14th century. He is credited with discovering the power series expansions for trigonometric functions sine, cosine, and arctangent.

Madhava is sometimes called the "Father of Indian Mathematics" and his work is credited with paving the way for the European Renaissance.

Madhava was born in a village called Tiruvannamalai in Tamil Nadu, India. His exact date of birth is not known, but it is estimated that he lived from 1350 to 1425.

Madhava's father was a Brahmin priest and his mother was a pious woman. Madhava's early education was priestly and he showed an aptitude for learning.

At the age of 16, Madhava went to Madras (now Chennai), the capital of Tamil Nadu, to study astronomy and mathematics under the guidance of Jain mathematicians.

It is said that Madhava's teachers were so impressed with his abilities that they predicted he would one day become famous.

After completing his studies, Madhava returned to his hometown and began to work on his own mathematical and astronomical treatises.

In 1380, Madhava wrote a treatise on astronomy called the "Mahajana Siddhanta". This work was an attempt to systematize Hindu astronomical knowledge and to correct some of the errors that had crept into it over the centuries.

In 1386, Madhava wrote a second treatise, the "Surya Siddhanta". This work was a more ambitious attempt to systematize Hindu astronomical knowledge and to provide more accurate predictions of planetary positions.

The "Surya Siddhanta" was influential for centuries and had a major impact on Indian astronomy.

In 1399, Madhava wrote his most famous work, the "Aryabhatiya". This work was a treatise on mathematics and astronomy.

In the "Aryabhatiya", Madhava gave the first known instance of a power series expansion for trigonometric functions. He also gave the first known evaluations of the infinite series for the sine, cosine, and arctangent functions.

These power series expansions were later rediscovered by European mathematicians in the 16th and 17th centuries and they played a crucial role in the development of calculus.

Ingredients:
- 2 lbs beef chuck, cut into 1-inch cubes
- 1 onion, chopped
- 4 garlic cloves, minced
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- 1 can coconut milk
- 2 cups beef broth
- 2 carrots, peeled and chopped
- 2 celery stalks, chopped
- 1 tsp dried thyme
- 1 tsp paprika
- 1/2 tsp cayenne pepper
- Salt and black pepper, to taste
- 1/2 cup salted peanuts, chopped

Instructions:

1. Press the "Sauté" button on the Instant Pot and heat the olive oil. Add the beef, onion, and garlic and cook until the beef is browned on all sides.

2. Add the coconut milk, beef broth, carrots, celery, thyme, paprika, cayenne pepper, salt, and black pepper to the Instant Pot. Stir to combine.

3. Close the lid and set the pressure release to "Sealing". Press the "Manual" or "Pressure Cook" button and set the cooking time to 40 minutes on high pressure.

4. When the timer goes off, let the pressure release naturally for 10 minutes before opening the valve to release any remaining pressure.

5. Stir in the chopped salted peanuts before serving. Enjoy your delicious Instant Pot Beef Stew with Coconut Milk and Salted Peanuts!
